title: How do construction induction cards and high risk work licences work in Victoria?
seoTitle: Victoria white card and HRW licences
description: Victoria's OHS Regulations 2017 rules for construction induction cards and high risk work licences: 2 year lapse, face to face training and telehandlers.
shortAnswer: Victoria is outside the model WHS laws, so construction induction and high risk work licensing come from the Occupational Health and Safety Regulations 2017 (Vic), administered by WorkSafe Victoria. A person must hold a current construction induction card to do construction work, and the card lapses after 2 consecutive years without construction work. High risk work licences, including telehandlers over 3 tonnes, last up to 5 years.
keyTakeaways: Regulation 340 prohibits construction work without a current construction induction card, and regulation 341 makes it an offence for an employer to knowingly allow it, with penalties of up to 100 penalty units for an individual and 500 for a body corporate.
WorkSafe Victoria only accepts construction induction training (CPCWHS1001) delivered face to face by an approved RTO, running at least 6 hours. Online white card courses are not accepted.
Under regulation 349 a construction induction card lapses if the holder has not performed construction work during any consecutive period of 2 years.
Victoria lists 30 high risk work licence classes, and since 2024 the non-slewing mobile crane licence also covers non-slewing telehandlers over 3 tonnes, which differs from New South Wales.
The OHS Regulations 2017 were extended and will now sunset on April 24, 2028, so a remade Victorian regulation is expected before then.
regulator: WorkSafe Victoria (Victorian WorkCover Authority), administering the Occupational Health and Safety Act 2004 (Vic) and the Occupational Health and Safety Regulations 2017 (Vic)
appliesTo: Employers and self employed persons with workers performing construction work in Victoria
Workers and apprentices on Victorian construction sites, including work experience students
Operators of cranes, hoists, forklifts, telehandlers, elevating work platforms, boilers and turbines, and scaffolders, doggers and riggers
Registered training organizations and authorized assessors delivering induction and licence assessments in Victoria

sections.heading: Why does Victoria have its own construction induction and licensing rules?

blocks.text: Victoria never adopted the harmonized model. [Safe Work Australia](https://www.safeworkaustralia.gov.au/law-and-regulation/history-model-whs-laws) states that Victoria "is the only jurisdiction who has not implemented the model WHS laws". Its rules come from the Occupational Health and Safety Act 2004 and the [Occupational Health and Safety Regulations 2017](https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/statutory-rules/occupational-health-and-safety-regulations-2017), which commenced on June 18, 2017.

The outcomes look similar to the model WHS scheme described in [general construction induction](/regulations/general-construction-induction-white-card) and [high risk work licence requirements](/regulations/high-risk-work-licence-requirements), but the regulation numbers, offences, penalty structure and several details differ. A national builder cannot reuse a model WHS compliance procedure in Victoria without checking each point.

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects version 018 of the OHS Regulations 2017, in force from October 20, 2026, and WorkSafe Victoria guidance as at November 2026. The endnotes record that the Regulations will sunset on April 24, 2028 under the Subordinate Legislation (Occupational Health and Safety Regulations 2017) Extension Regulations 2026, so replacement regulations, and new numbering, should be expected.

sections.heading: What do the Regulations require for construction induction?

blocks.text: Division 3 of Part 5.1 places a duty on both the worker and the employer. Regulation 339 requires an employer to ensure construction induction training is provided by a construction RTO, before work starts, to any employee who will perform construction work and does not hold a current card. Regulation 340 says a person must not perform construction work unless they hold a current construction induction card.

Regulation 341 makes it an offence for an employer to knowingly allow an employee to perform construction work without a current card, with a maximum of 100 penalty units for a natural person and 500 for a body corporate. It expressly extends to students placed under a work experience arrangement under the Education and Training Reform Act 2006. Regulation 343 also makes it an offence to knowingly refuse to accept a valid card, a recent statement of attainment, or recognized interstate evidence.

Division 3 applies to everyone at a workplace where construction work is performed, except visitors who are accompanied at all times by someone who has done the training, and people temporarily on site to deliver plant, supplies or materials (regulation 338).

sections.heading: What counts as approved construction induction training in Victoria?

blocks.text: [WorkSafe Victoria](https://www.worksafe.vic.gov.au/construction-induction-training-white-card) requires construction induction training to be conducted face to face in a classroom, and states that it "is not permitted to be delivered online". Only training from an approved RTO leads to a card issued by WorkSafe Victoria.

items: The unit is CPCWHS1001 (or CPCCWHS1001) Prepare to work safely in the construction industry, or its successor.
The course runs for a minimum of 6 hours, and photo identification is required at registration and on the day.
The RTO applies to WorkSafe on the learner's behalf, and the card can take up to 60 days to arrive.
WorkSafe flags online white card courses, courses under 6 hours and very cheap courses advertised without RTO details as likely not to result in a Victorian card.

blocks.text: While waiting for the card, regulation 342(2) lets a person work for 60 days after the construction statement of attainment is issued. A new starter who has not done construction work in the preceding 2 years can also work for up to 28 days if the employer applies and pays for the training within that period and provides direct supervision, directions and monitoring.

sections.heading: Does a Victorian construction induction card expire?

blocks.text: The card has no expiry date, but it can lapse. Regulation 347 says a card is "of unlimited duration", subject to regulation 349, which provides that if the holder has not performed construction work during a consecutive period of 2 years, the card lapses and is no longer current at the end of that period.

This matters for workers returning to the industry after a career break. Their card may look valid, yet they cannot lawfully do construction work until they retrain. Employers should therefore record recent construction work history at induction, not just sight the card. The card itself is evidence that the person completed construction induction training (regulation 346(3)), and the application fee is set at 1.8 fee units (regulation 344).

sections.heading: Which jobs need a high risk work licence in Victoria?

blocks.text: Regulation 128 prohibits performing high risk work without an appropriate licence, and regulation 129 prohibits an employer from allowing an unlicensed employee to do it, again with a maximum of 100 penalty units for an individual and 500 for a body corporate. [WorkSafe Victoria](https://www.worksafe.vic.gov.au/high-risk-work-licence) lists 30 licence classes covering scaffolding, dogging and rigging, boilers, turbines and steam engines, cranes and hoists, reach stackers, boom type elevating work platforms, concrete placing booms and forklifts.

The 30th class is the main point of difference from other states. Since amendments made by S.R. No. 4/2024, the scope of the non-slewing mobile crane licence in Schedule 3 includes non-slewing telehandlers, and the definition of non-slewing mobile crane includes a non-slewing telehandler with a rated capacity of more than 3 tonnes. WorkSafe lists this as the non-slewing telehandler operation licence, code TV. WorkSafe also notes that earthmoving equipment such as excavators, and scissor lifts, do not need a high risk work licence.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry stores jurisdiction as an attribute of each credential, so a Victorian construction induction card, its 2 year lapse rule and Victorian licence class codes sit next to the model WHS equivalents without being confused with them. Site specific knowledge and [verification of competency](/glossary/verification-of-competency) are then linked to the role, not the state. See how this applies to [energy and resources organizations](/industries/energy-resources).

faqs.q: Is an interstate white card accepted in Victoria?
faqs.a: Regulation 342(4) exempts a person holding recognized evidence of construction induction training if no more than 2 years have passed since it was issued, or they have done construction work in the preceding 2 years. Regulation 343 makes it an offence for an employer to knowingly refuse to accept recognized evidence.

faqs.q: Are interstate high risk work licences valid in Victoria?
faqs.a: Yes, in most cases. Regulation 131 treats an equivalent licence issued by a corresponding authority as a high risk work licence if it is used within its conditions, recognized by the issuer as current, and not suspended. WorkSafe also lets Victorian residents transfer an interstate licence within 12 months of its expiry.

faqs.q: Can old Victorian certificates of competency still be used?
faqs.a: No. WorkSafe Victoria states that competency certificates and older certificates issued under previous Victorian legislation have expired and cannot be used for high risk work. Holders of pre 1995 certificates must complete training and assessment and apply for a new high risk work licence.

faqs.q: Does a rigger need a crane licence to set up a crane in Victoria?
faqs.a: No. Regulation 130(3) says a rigging licence holder does not also need a crane or hoist licence to set up or dismantle a crane or hoist where operating it is integral to that task, and regulation 130(5) gives employers the matching exception.
